stories.title: Why George Town stands out among UNESCO cities: It still belongs to Penangites, not tourists
stories.summary: George Town’s UNESCO heritage status has boosted tourism and the local economy while preserving traditional trades and minimising gentrification. Penang’s government and Think City focus on urban renewal and liveability, balancing heritage conservation with modern needs. Restorations like Fort Cornwallis enhance both cultural value and community wellbeing, keeping George Town a vibrant home for residents and businesses. It has been 18 years since the historic towns of George Town and Melaka were inscribed as UNESCO heritage sites, driving a boom in their cultural economies. But while both Penang and Melaka states have benefited from tourism dollars, George Town’s careful management of its heritage has helped it retain its sense of place. Local residents and businesses have not simply been displaced by the influx of visitors and investment; many have ridden the rising tide while continuing to call the city home. The 2008 inscription brought more visitors and investment to Penang, but George Town has avoided becoming a heritage theme park. Generations-old businesses, associations, hawkers and residents still occupy its historic core, where some buildings date back more than two centuries – a distinction that sets it apart from some other UNESCO-listed cities where tourism has displaced much of the original community. “A space has layers of history, stories. It’s about people. It’s about what creates that identity. It’s the spirit of the place,” said Hamdan Majeed, managing director of urban impact organisation Think City.

stories.title: Research directions for North Pole·43 expedition outlined
stories.summary: Director of the Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute Alexander Makarov noted that the scientific program will primarily include oceanology, geophysics, and atmospheric research
article_sentences: The research directions for the scientific expedition North Pole·43 have been established with the program including more than 50 projects, Alexander Makarov, Director of the Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute (AARI), Doctor of Geographical Sciences, Professor of the Russian Academy of Sciences, said in an interview with TASS.
"The research directions for the North Pole·43 expedition have been defined.

The scientific program will primarily include oceanology, geophysics, and atmospheric research," Makarov said, adding that a separate track of research will be devoted to mapping the seabed of the Arctic Ocean.
"We will pay special attention to studying the climate change, heat and mass transfer processes between the ocean and the atmosphere, and ice research.
Joint work on the study of biodiversity will continue.
This is just a small list, with more than 50 different scientific tasks in the program."
